passage: I'm Payal, and I watched my little sister Indu's sports day from the stands. The teacher handed out bibs from a basket without looking: red or yellow. Indu got yellow. Two minutes later she was jumping up and down, shouting, "Yellow is the best! Yellow is the fastest!" Her friend Moti got red, and Indu stuck her tongue out. They had shared a tiffin that very morning. In the tug-of-war the yellows chanted, "Red is slow!" Indu screamed loudest. Afterwards she told me, very seriously, "Yellow people are better." Nobody had chosen anything. The bibs came out of a basket.

qa.q: How were the bibs handed out?
qa.a: From a basket without looking.

qa.q: What does Indu's 'Yellow people are better' suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt proud and attached to her team, as if being yellow made her part of something better.

qa.q: What could the teacher try next sports day so the fun of teams doesn't turn into teasing?
qa.a: Mix the bibs between races and cheer both colours, so children enjoy belonging without looking down on the other side.

qa.q: What might Moti feel when Indu sticks her tongue out, after they shared a tiffin that morning?
qa.a: Moti may feel hurt and confused that a friend turned against Moti just because of a bib.

grounding: An older sister watches a five-year-old cheer her randomly assigned colour as the best and tease a friend on the other team.

passage: Monday. Anjali Miss handed out bibs from a box without looking: green or blue. Elizabeth, five, got green and hugged her bib like a present. Wednesday. At the races Elizabeth shouted, "Green wins! Blue is babies!" The greens laughed and held hands. The blue children frowned. Friday. Anjali Miss said, "New week, new teams," and gave out bibs again. Elizabeth got blue. For a moment she looked stricken. Then she pulled it on, ran to the blue side and shouted, "Blue is the best!" Anjali Miss hid a smile.

qa.q: What colour did Elizabeth get on Friday?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when she first got a green bib?
qa.a: She was delighted and proud, hugging it like a present.

qa.q: Why was Anjali Miss's choice to change teams on Friday a good one?
qa.a: It showed the children that teams are just bibs from a box, so 'blue is babies' can't stick to anyone.

qa.q: How might the blue children have felt on Wednesday?
qa.a: They likely felt teased and cross, being called babies for a colour they didn't choose.

grounding: A five-year-old given a random bib quickly decides her colour is best and teases the other side, then does the same for her new colour.

passage: Rain drove sports hour into the small school hall, where the floor was slippery. Miss tied red ribbons on half the class and blue on the rest, just by where they sat. Charu, six, got red. Her best friend Lavanya got blue. "Red team! Red team!" Charu chanted. By the second game she wouldn't pass the beanbag to Lavanya. "You're blue. Blue people cheat." Lavanya's lip wobbled. "I'm not a cheater. I'm Lavanya." Charu stopped, beanbag in hand. Miss called, "Everyone into a circle, reds and blues mixed." Charu sat down next to Lavanya, unsure, still holding her red ribbon.

qa.q: Where did sports hour take place because of the rain?
qa.a: In the small school hall.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she stopped with the beanbag in her hand?
qa.a: She seemed unsure, caught by Lavanya's words and realising her friend was not a 'blue cheater'.

qa.q: What choice did Miss make, and why might it help?
qa.a: Miss had everyone sit in a mixed circle, reminding them that reds and blues are all one class.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's 'I'm not a cheater. I'm Lavanya' show about how Lavanya felt?
qa.a: Lavanya felt hurt at being treated as just 'blue' and wanted to be seen as a friend again.

grounding: A six-year-old handed a random ribbon quickly sees her team as better and turns on her best friend in the other colour.

passage: At the colony summer camp in Chennai, the leader shook a cloth bag of caps. "Close your eyes and pick!" Mridul, five, pulled out orange. His neighbour Sumit got purple. The oranges jumped in a huddle. "Orange is the smartest!" Mridul shouted, though nobody had found any treasure yet. When the leader said, "Hold hands with a partner," Mridul would not take Sumit's hand. "You're purple." Sumit, who shared his cycle with Mridul every evening, looked at his cap and then at Mridul. At the end the leader collected the caps. Mridul held his tight behind his back.

qa.q: How did the children get their caps?
qa.a: The leader shook a cloth bag and each child closed their eyes and picked one.

qa.q: How can you tell Mridul already feels he belongs to the orange group?
qa.a: He feels proud of being orange, shouting that orange is the smartest before any treasure is found and holding his cap tight when the caps are collected.

qa.q: What could the camp leader do when Mridul refuses Sumit's hand?
qa.a: The leader could remind them the caps came out of a bag by chance and pair oranges with purples for the next game, so the children mix again.

qa.q: What is it like for Sumit when Mridul won't hold his hand?
qa.a: Sumit is confused and probably hurt, because the two share a cycle every evening and now a cap he picked by chance has turned him into an outsider.

grounding: A five-year-old given a cap colour by chance quickly decides his colour is best and treats a friend in the other colour as 'them'.

passage: "Papa, I'm a Star!" Usha waved her hand. A shiny sticker sat on it. "A star? What for?" "For the Stars team. We're the best team." "Best at what?" "Everything." Usha climbed onto her chair. "The Moons are silly." Papa passed the dal. "Is Imran a Moon?" "Yes." "But you sit with Imran every day." Usha frowned. "Not today. Stars sit with Stars." "How did you become a Star?" "Miss gave stickers from a box. I got a star." "So if you got a moon?" Usha looked at her sticker. "Then... Moons are the best?" She did not sound sure.

qa.q: What was on Usha's hand when she came to the table?
qa.a: A shiny star sticker was on her hand.

qa.q: Why does Usha frown when Papa says she sits with Imran every day?
qa.a: She feels torn, because she likes Imran but now believes Stars should only sit with Stars.

qa.q: Which question from Papa helped Usha stop and think, and why?
qa.a: Asking what would happen if she had got a moon made her see the teams came from a box by chance, so being a Star is not what makes someone best.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when Usha would not sit with him?
qa.a: Imran might have felt left out and puzzled, since they sit together every day and nothing changed except a sticker.

grounding: A young child given a team sticker at random quickly believes her team is best and stops sitting with a friend from the other team.

passage: On sports morning at Little Lotus school, the teacher pulls bibs from a basket without looking: red, blue, red, blue. Nikita, five, gets red. Her best friend Zainab gets blue. Within minutes Nikita is jumping up and down. "Red is the best! Red is fastest!" When the teacher asks everyone to hold hands in a circle, Nikita steps away from Zainab. "You're blue," she says. Zainab's lip trembles. At snack time, the bibs come off, and Nikita shares her biscuits with Zainab again as if nothing happened.

qa.q: What colour bib does Zainab get?
qa.a: Zainab gets blue.

qa.q: What does Nikita's jumping and shouting show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows Nikita feels excited and proud to be on the red team, even though the bibs were given out at random.

qa.q: How could the teacher help the children after this?
qa.a: The teacher could mix the colours for the next game and point out that bibs were picked from a basket, so no colour is really better.

qa.q: How does Zainab feel when Nikita steps away?
qa.a: Zainab feels hurt and confused, her lip trembling because her best friend suddenly treats her as the other side.

grounding: Children given random coloured bibs quickly cheer for their own colour and treat a friend in another colour as "them".

passage:
Monday: In the park's summer camp, Gurleen, five, gets a yellow bib and Vijay, six, a green one. By lunch Gurleen is shouting, "Yellow team rocks!"
Wednesday: Yellow wins the sack race. Gurleen tells Vijay, "Green is slow." Vijay stamps his foot and won't share his crayons.
Friday: The leader swaps the bibs. Now Gurleen is green. She stares at the bib, frowning, then shouts, "Green is best!" Vijay, now yellow, laughs.

qa.q: What colour is Gurleen's bib on Friday?
qa.a: Now Gurleen is green.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he stamped his foot on Wednesday?
qa.a: Vijay felt hurt and annoyed at being told his team was slow, so he refused to share.

qa.q: What could the camp leader do to ease the us-and-them feeling?
qa.a: The leader could talk about how the bibs are swapped at random, and set some games where both colours work together.

qa.q: What might change for Gurleen after seeing that her team could switch?
qa.a: Gurleen might start to notice that the colour doesn't make anyone better, though she still enjoys belonging to a team.

grounding: Over a week, children given random bibs quickly cheer for their colour and scorn the other, even switching loyalty when bibs are swapped.

passage: Rain had cancelled the outdoor games at the community centre, so all twenty children were squeezed into one hall. The helper handed out bibs from a bag: orange or purple. Abhinav, six, got orange. Ganga, five, got purple. Soon the orange children were chanting "Orange! Orange!" and the purple ones shouted back. Abhinav refused to pass the ball to Ganga during the relay. "You're not on my team!" he said, even though they'd walked to the centre together that morning under the same umbrella. When the rain stopped and everyone took the bibs off, Abhinav picked up Ganga's shoe for her and they walked home together.

qa.q: How many children were squeezed into one hall?
qa.a: All twenty children were squeezed into one hall.

qa.q: What does Abhinav's refusal to pass the ball suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Abhinav felt loyal and proud of the orange team, strongly enough to treat Ganga as a rival.

qa.q: How could the helper reduce the rivalry in the crowded hall?
qa.a: The helper could run a game where orange and purple must work together, reminding them the bibs came out of a bag.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel when Abhinav won't pass the ball?
qa.a: Ganga might feel left out and puzzled, since they walked there together that morning.

grounding: On a rainy day, children given random bibs quickly form teams and treat each other as rivals, until the bibs come off.

passage:
It poured all through August, so the colony games moved into the community hall. The coach pulled bibs from a sack without looking: red, yellow, red, yellow.
Tanvir got red. His best friend Varun got yellow.
Within a minute Tanvir was jumping. "Red is the best! Red is fastest!"
The red children shouted it too. Varun frowned. "Yellow is better."
"No! Yellow is slow," Tanvir said, and moved to the red side of the hall, away from Varun.
At snack time, Tanvir looked at the yellow bib on his friend and didn't sit next to him.

qa.q: How did the coach choose the bibs?
qa.a: The coach pulled bibs from a sack without looking.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir jump and shout that red is the best?
qa.a: Being on the red team made him feel excited and proud, as if red was his special group.

qa.q: How could the coach help the children stay friends across colours?
qa.a: The coach could mix the teams again for the next game, or remind them the colours were picked from a sack, so red and yellow children play together.

qa.q: What is it like for Varun when Tanvir doesn't sit next to him?
qa.a: Varun likely feels hurt and confused, because a bib from a sack has turned his best friend away from him.

grounding: Shows young children who were handed coloured bibs at random quickly deciding their colour is best and splitting into us and them.

passage:
"Ammi, I'm on the blue team at the New Year party!" Wasim shouted, running in with a paper crown.
"And I'm green," said Sabina, "and green won the balloon game."
"Blue is better. Blue is the sky."
"Green is the trees. Trees are bigger."
"Blue is best!"
"How did you get blue, Wasim?" asked Ammi.
"The aunty gave crowns from a box."
"So if she gave you green, you'd love green?"
Wasim thought. "No. Blue is best."
Sabina stuck out her tongue. "Blue team is babies."
"Green team is smelly!"
Ammi sighed. "Brother and sister, and now enemies because of a paper crown."

qa.q: What did the aunty give the crowns from?
qa.a: She gave crowns from a box.

qa.q: What does Wasim's answer "No. Blue is best" suggest he feels?
qa.a: He feels proud and attached to the blue team, even though the crown came from a box by chance.

qa.q: What could Ammi try so the children see their teams more lightly?
qa.a: She could let them swap crowns for a while, so they see that blue and green were only chance, not who they really are.

qa.q: How does Ammi see the fight?
qa.a: Ammi feels amused and a little tired, noticing that a brother and sister have become rivals over paper crowns.

grounding: Shows young siblings put on colour teams by chance at a party who quickly decide their own team is best and tease the other.

passage:
Onam week, Class UKG. Note by the class teacher.
We played a flower-carpet game in two groups. Children drew chits: orange or green. Ayesha drew orange, Avni drew green.
By the end of the game, the orange group had made a chant, "Orange is the winner!" Ayesha shouted loudest, waving her arms. When Avni reached for the orange petals, Ayesha said, "No, that's only for us." Avni went quiet, her lip shaking.
After the game I asked the children how they got their colour. Ayesha said, "From a chit." I asked if petals should belong to one group. Ayesha gave Avni a handful. They finished the carpet together.

qa.q: What colour chit did Ayesha draw?
qa.a: Ayesha drew orange.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha say the petals were "only for us"?
qa.a: She felt proud and excited to belong to the orange group and suddenly saw Avni as one of the others.

qa.q: How did the teacher's question about the chits help?
qa.a: It reminded the children that their groups came from chance, so Ayesha could see Avni as her friend again and share.

qa.q: What is it like for Avni when Ayesha keeps the orange petals from her?
qa.a: Avni feels shut out and hurt, and goes quiet, because her usual friend now treats her as an outsider.

grounding: Shows a young child in a randomly assigned group quickly feeling her group is best and treating a friend from the other group as an outsider.

passage: On Republic Day morning the village school gave out bibs from a sack without looking: red or blue. Nandini got red. Her best friend Rehana got blue. By the first race Nandini was jumping up and down. 'Red is the best! Red is fastest!' Rehana stuck out her tongue. 'Blue is best. Red is for tomatoes.' They had shared a slate that very morning. Now they sat on opposite sides of the line, cheering and booing. When a red boy tripped, Rehana clapped. At lunch, bibs off, they shared their parathas again as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: How were the bibs given out?
qa.a: From a sack without looking.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel after getting a red bib?
qa.a: Nandini felt excited and proud, jumping and shouting that red was the best.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to keep the fun but soften the booing?
qa.a: Cheer good running from both colours and mix the teams in the next game, so the children see the colours don't make anyone better.

qa.q: What would change if Nandini and Rehana had both got red?
qa.a: They would probably have cheered together instead of booing each other, since the colour alone split them.

grounding: On a village sports day two young friends given random bibs instantly cheer their own colour and boo the other.

passage: On the snow day at the Oslo kindergarten, the teacher pulled coloured hats from a basket without looking: yellow or green. Lars got yellow. Hana got green. Within five minutes Lars was shouting, 'Yellow team is the strongest!' and building a snow wall with the other yellows. Hana and the greens built their own wall across the yard. 'Greens are babies!' called a yellow boy. Hana marched over, cheeks red. 'Greens are better! We have Hana!' When the teacher asked Lars why yellow was better, he thought hard. 'Because I'm yellow,' he said, as if that settled it.

qa.q: What did the teacher pull from the basket?
qa.a: Coloured hats, yellow or green.

qa.q: How did Hana feel when a yellow boy called the greens babies?
qa.a: Hana felt angry and protective of her team, cheeks red, marching over to defend it.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next?
qa.a: Mix the colours for a new game or give both walls a shared goal, like building one big castle together.

qa.q: How might the teacher see the children's quick loyalty?
qa.a: The teacher might find it funny but notice how fast random hats made each child feel their side was best.

grounding: On a snow day abroad young children given random hat colours quickly decide their own team is best.

passage: The week before Diwali, Miss Joshi handed out orange and purple bibs for the relay, straight out of the box. Reena got orange, Zeenat purple. At snacks Reena spread her mat and said, 'Only oranges sit here.' Zeenat, who sat with her every single day, stood holding her tiffin. 'But I'm your friend.' 'You're purple,' Reena said, as if it were a rule. Miss Joshi knelt down. 'Who decided who got which colour?' Reena thought. 'You did. From the box.' 'So is purple worse?' Reena looked at Zeenat's bib, then moved over. 'Purples can sit too.'

qa.q: What colours were the bibs?
qa.a: Orange and purple.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when she said 'Only oranges sit here'?
qa.a: Reena felt proud of her orange team and sure it came first, as if belonging made a rule.

qa.q: What did Miss Joshi's questions help Reena notice?
qa.a: That the colours came at random from a box, so purple wasn't worse and the new rule made no sense.

qa.q: What is it like for Zeenat to be told 'You're purple'?
qa.a: Zeenat feels hurt and confused, shut out by a friend over a colour she didn't choose.

grounding: In a preschool before Diwali a girl given a random bib colour quickly makes it an 'us and them' rule.

passage:
Monday, cold and foggy. The teacher pulls bibs from a bag without looking: red for Farida, blue for Vikas. Farida hugs her red bib to her chest.
Wednesday. At practice Farida shouts, "Red is the fastest! Red is the best!" She will not share crayons with the blue table. "Blue is slow," she tells Vikas. Vikas sticks out his tongue.
Friday, sports day. Red loses the sack race. Farida's lip wobbles. Then the teacher mixes everyone up for the tug of war, and Farida pulls right next to Vikas, both of them yelling.

qa.q: What colour bib did Farida get?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: How does Farida feel when red loses the sack race?
qa.a: She feels sad and disappointed 😢, her lip wobbling, because she had decided red was the best team.

qa.q: What did the mixed tug of war do, and why does it help?
qa.a: Putting everyone into one team let Farida and Vikas pull side by side, softening the red-versus-blue feeling.

qa.q: How does Vikas feel when Farida calls blue slow?
qa.a: Vikas feels annoyed and sticks out his tongue, though he was put in blue by chance just as she was put in red.

grounding: Children given bibs at random quickly decide their own colour is best, until a mixed game brings them together.
